are not the ones who commit the most violent crimes, but those
who possess the greatest ingenuity. Those who are able to devise
the most subtle and ingenious plots to escape justice are the
ones who do the most damage. They do it for greed. They do it for
power. They do it because it gives them a strange sense of
satisfaction to feel their intellect is superior to that of the
law."

"But it is the truth. The nature of man is the same everywhere.
The greater the isolation of the place, the more does that nature
show itself. The restraints of civilization are removed. We
become primitive beings. Our passions, whether for good or for
evil, are enhanced in their intensity. In the case of Miss
Hunter, I suspect that she will find that the nature of the
country is not quite as beautiful as she imagined. The telegram
was certainly urgent enough."

"But the reason is very obvious. The pressure of public opinion
can do in the town what the law cannot accomplish. There is no
lane so vile that the scream of a tortured child, or the thud of
a drunkard's blow, does not beget sympathy and indignation among
the neighbours, and then the whole machinery of justice is ever
so close that a word of complaint can set it going, and there is
but a step between the crime and the dock. But look at these
lonely houses, each in its own fields, filled for the most part
with poor ignorant folk who know little of the law. Think of the
deeds of hellish cruelty, the hidden wickedness which may go on,
year in, year out, in such places, and none the wiser. Had this
lady who appeals to us for help gone to live in Winchester, I
should never have had a fear for her. It is the five miles of
country which makes the danger. Still, it is clear that she is
not personally threatened."

"No. If she can come to Winchester to meet us she can get away."

"Quite so. She has her freedom."

"What CAN be the matter, then? Can you suggest no explanation?"

"I arrived at the Copper Beeches, as you know, yesterday
morning. It is a most curious place, standing alone in a rather
extensive but very neglected garden. It is a large square house,
of grey stone, with rows of very high windows. The front door is
in a deep recess, and there is a stone bench beside it. It is a
gloomy, isolated spot, though it has a certain fascination. I
was met, as I expected, by Mr. Rucastle, who drove me to the house
in a dog-cart. He was very cordial and seemed quite pleased at
my arrival."

"I arrived at the Copper Beeches," began Miss Hunter, "on
Wednesday last, and met Mr. Rucastle, who drove me in his dog-cart
from the station. He was very civil, and even amiable, and we
talked about a great many things on the way. He seemed very
pleased to see me, and expressed his satisfaction in the most
decided manner, both in words and in look. I had cut my hair
short, as he had requested, and he complimented me on the change,
saying that it made me look very much younger."

"A very necessary compliment," remarked Holmes dryly.

"I arrived at Winchester yesterday afternoon," said Miss Hunter,
"and took a fly to the Copper Beeches. It is a very large,
handsome house, though it is somewhat old-fashioned. It stands
among high-reaching trees, which quite surround it, and it looks
as if it might have been a baronial residence in former days. I
was met by Mr. Rucastle, who was very cordial and pleasant. He
showed me the way to my room, which was a very charming one, all
done in blue, and furnished with a beautiful old four-post bed,
which seemed to me to be far too grand for a mere governess.

"I arrived at Winchester yesterday afternoon, and I drove out to
The Copper Beeches in a dog-cart, as you advised me. The house
is quite alone, standing well back from the road, quite a long
way from the village, and the drive is long and winding. It is
a very old, rambling house, and it has an air of gloom and
desolation about it which is quite depressing. However, I was
pleased enough to get there, for I had been rather anxious
during my journey. I was met by the maid, who showed me my room,
and then Mr. Rucastle appeared, and he was very kind and
pleasant, though he seemed to me to be much older than I had
imagined from his letter. In fact, he seemed to be a very old
man, for his hair was almost white."

"I arrived at the Copper Beeches, as you know, yesterday, and I
found it to be a very beautiful house, standing well back from
the road, quite isolated and surrounded by its own grounds. There
was a copper beech just opposite the front door, and I had
already noticed its peculiar beauty from the railway carriage. Mr.
Rucastle met me as I stepped from the dog-cart, and he was
certainly a most amiable person. He took me into the drawing-room,
which was large, but sparsely furnished, and introduced me to his
wife. It was only then that I realized that his previous
statements had not been altogether accurate."

"In the first place, I may say that I have met, on the whole,
with no actual ill-treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle. It is
only fair to them to say that. But I cannot understand them, and
I am not easy in my mind about them."

"What can you not understand?"

"The house is very large, much larger than it looks from the
outside, and it is all old and rambling. There are many long
corridors and passages, and I have never quite found my way about
it yet. My bedroom is a very good one, on the first floor; it has
two windows looking towards the front. It is furnished in a
rich, heavy style; but there is something strange and uncanny
about the place, which I cannot explain. There are no pictures on
the walls; the mirrors are covered with cloths; and there are
long, thick curtains which entirely conceal the two windows. I
felt, even before I saw the grounds, that I was being watched."

"The house is very large, much larger than it looks from the
outside, but it is very sparsely furnished. There are three
bedrooms, one large and two small, a dining-room, a drawing-room,
and a large kitchen, which is in charge of Mrs. Toller, the
housekeeper, who is a woman of about fifty, with a sour face, and
a pair of remarkable eyes.  The rest of the establishment consists
of Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle and their child, young Harold, and
myself."

"The house is a very old one, and it is as dreary as it is
ugly. There are no cheerful rooms in it, but long, low-studded
chambers with heavy oak beams across the ceiling. The bedroom
which was given me was the very worst in the house. It was on the
ground-floor, and I had to pass through a long, dark corridor to
reach it. All my windows looked upon the woods, and though the
view was charming it was, I confess, a rather gloomy place to
spend a long evening. My hair had been cut short, but I did not
think so much of that, but what did annoy me was the dress which
they had put me into. It was an old one of Miss Rucastle's, and
it suited me very badly. The colour was what my employer called
electric blue, but I should have called it a dull, muddy
purple."

"The house is very old. It is full of long passages and winding
stairs, and I could not but notice that the doors were all
locked, or bolted, or fastened in some way. I found it very
difficult at first to find my way about. My bedroom is a very
pleasant one, on the first floor, and from my window I can see
the highroad and the woods. My sitting-room is also on the first
floor. It is a large room, and is furnished all in old-fashioned
style with a great deal of dark, heavy furniture. There is a
sofa, several chairs, a grand piano, and a large writing-table.
It was my business, of course, to look after young Victor, and I
found him a charming child, but very lonely. He is always alone,
for the servants are kept downstairs.

"The house is very old. It is full of winding passages and
chambers, and the furniture is all old and worn, and the
pictures are all cracked and dirty, except one, of a young girl
which stands over the mantelpiece in my room. It is very beautiful,
and is painted in a style that is quite new to me. The whole house
has a most peculiar smell, as of dust and damp and decay. The
only pleasant place in it is my bedroom, which is large and airy,
and has a beautiful view from the window."

"I was driven over by my employer, who was as amiable as ever,
and was introduced by him that evening to his wife and the child.
There was no truth, Mr. Holmes, in the conjecture which seemed to
us to be probable in your rooms at Baker Street. Mrs. Rucastle is
not mad. I found her to be a silent, pale-faced woman, much
younger than her husband, not more than thirty, I should think,
while he can hardly be less than forty-five. From their
conversation I have gathered that they have been married about
seven years, that he was a widower, and that his only child by
the first wife was the daughter who has gone to Philadelphia. Mr.
Rucastle told me in private that the reason why she had left them
was that she had an unreasoning aversion to her stepmother. As
the daughter could not have been less than twenty, I can quite
imagine that her position must have been uncomfortable with her
father's young wife.

"Very well, then. I will continue. The most curious incident
occurred on the very first night. I had been shown to my room,
which was a charming one, with a view over the woods, and after
I had unpacked my things I was about to go downstairs when my
attention was drawn to the window. It was open and a long, thin
strip of paper was fluttering across the lower sash. I secured
it, and found that it was a note. I may say that I am
unaccustomed to receive notes from unknown people, and this
incident struck me as peculiar. It was written in pencil, and the
only words upon it were: 'Keep your hair short.'


"Well, I thought little of the matter at the time, but as it
was the very thing which I had refused to do, and which had so
disappointed Mr. Rucastle, I began to wonder whether it could
have any connection with him. It did not occur to me, I must
confess, that it was any possible threat. I thought it was more
likely to be some harmless whim of the strange people with whom
I had found myself."

"Very well, then. I may say that I have never been in a house
where such extraordinary things occurred. The most singular
circumstances were constantly happening. For example, I was
ordered to wear an electric blue dress every morning, and, as I
had none such, Mrs. Rucastle insisted on my wearing one of her
daughter's, which was far too large for me, and which, of course,
made me look ridiculous. Then, again, I was told to sit in one
particular chair by the fire, and not to move from it without
permission. Yet I found that if I did take a book and go to the
window, or even to another chair, there would be no notice taken.
The instructions seemed to be quite arbitrary. It was mere
wilfulness."

"But why did they give you such a high salary?" I asked.

"That I cannot explain. They gave it to me, and I accepted it.
They were kind to me in many ways. They did not treat me harshly.
And yet I know not why I should feel uneasy."


"Very well, then.  I may say that my life at the Copper Beeches
has been, so far, a very pleasant one. My duties are easy, my
salary is high, and my hours are my own.  Mr. Rucastle is
considerate, and, as I have said, his wife is a kind woman.  The
child is, of course, trying, but his mother attends to most of
his whims.  However, there is something which puzzles me very much.  I
cannot make it out at all.  Every night, just after dark, Mr.
Rucastle leaves the house. He does not say where he goes. He says
it is only a short walk, and he is always back before midnight."

"Very well, then. I had been at the Copper Beeches for a week,
and was beginning to feel quite comfortable in my new surroundings,
when one morning Mr. Rucastle came into my room and told me that
his wife wished to see me. I found her in the drawing-room,
dressed in a sort of sea-green dressing-gown, very pale and
nervous, with dark rings round her eyes. She gave a start when
I came in, and held out her hand to me, asking me to sit down.
She had been crying, and her face was all swollen.

"'I want you to do something for me,' said she. 'I am in great
trouble.'

"'What can I do to help you?' I asked.

"'I want you to do a very curious thing. I want you to wear a
dress of mine--a blue dress--every morning, and to sit in a
certain chair which I will show you for an hour. I don't want
you to speak to anyone--or if you do speak, to say only what
I tell you.'

"'Why would you want me to do this?' I asked.

'You shall understand all in good time,' said she. 'But if you
are obedient and do what I ask, I will give you a reward.  I will
give you 500 pounds when you leave us.'

"Very well, then. I will continue. My duties were, as you
perceived, of the lightest. I had to teach the child, who was
however, too idle to learn. I had to take charge of his
amusements, which were chiefly of a cruel character. I had to
superintend his meals, a task which was not rendered easy by his
obstinate refusal to eat anything which he was not himself
allowed to choose. And I had to see that he was properly dressed
and put to bed at night. At first I was a little surprised at
the small amount of work which I had to do. But I soon got used
to it, and in other respects I had nothing to complain of. My
bedroom was charming, a large airy room looking out upon the
woods. My salary was paid punctually. Mrs. Rucastle was kind to
me, and Mr. Rucastle was always genial. The only strange thing
was that my employer always insisted upon my wearing that absurd
blue dress every morning. We had a huge wardrobe full of old
clothing, and he made me choose that particular one from the many
that were there."

"Did you do so?"

"Yes, I wore it every day."

"And the short hair?"

"That was the most curious thing of all, Mr. Holmes. When I had
been a week in the house Mr. Rucastle asked me one day to cut my
hair. My hair has always been a great pride to me. He had been
watching me eagerly out of his small eyes, and I could see a
shadow pass over his face as I spoke. I could not think of
sacrificing it. And he said it was a little fancy of his wife's.
So, to please them, and because I knew it would not hurt me, I
agreed."

"And did you do it?"

"Yes, I cut it off."


"I shall try not to miss anything of importance. The one
unpleasant thing about the house, which struck me at once, was
the appearance and conduct of the servants. There are only two, a
man and his wife. Toller, for that is his name, is a rough,
uncouth man, with grizzled hair and whiskers, and a perpetual
smell of drink. Twice since I have been with them he has been
quite drunk, and yet Mr. Rucastle seemed to take no notice of it.
His wife is a very tall and strong woman with a sour face, as
silent as Mrs. Rucastle and much less amiable. They are a most
unpleasant couple, but fortunately I spend most of my time in the
nursery and my own room, which are next to each other in one
corner of the building.

"For two days after my arrival at the Copper Beeches my life was
very quiet; on the third, Mrs. Rucastle came down just after
breakfast and whispered something to her husband.

"I went to my room and found the dress laid out as he had
described. It was indeed of a beautiful electric blue, and
looked uncommonly well upon the bed. It was of soft silk, and
would naturally have been an expensive dress. I tried it on, and
it fitted me perfectly, though I observed that the collar was
rather high and close round the throat.

"Mr. Rucastle seemed quite delighted when I came down in the new
dress.  He was even more genial and more garrulous than before.
He took me into the dining-room, where a light lunch awaited us.
During the meal he chattered incessantly about the great things
which were in store for his son and heir.

"When the meal was over, Mrs. Rucastle rose and left the room.
She returned in a few minutes with a little square box in her hand.
My employer's eyes glittered as she gave it to him. He opened it
and looked at the contents. It was apparently a small jewel, or
possibly a curious piece of metal, which was held in place by
fine wires that were intertwined and attached to the lid of the
box. I shall never forget the strange look upon my employer's face
as he gazed at this trinket."

"I went to my room and found the dress laid out as he had said.
It was of a peculiar shade, a sort of bright blue, with a
shimmering, lustrous surface. It was of good material, too, and
well made, and it fitted me perfectly, though it was difficult
to understand how it should happen to suit me so well, since
Mr. Rucastle had said that it had belonged to his daughter. I
put it on, as requested, and then went downstairs.  When I came
into the drawing-room both Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle were there, but
their eyes were fixed upon something which stood beside the
fireplace. It was the child's chair, and in that chair,
dressed in my electric-blue dress, sat the child himself."

"I went to my room and found a beautiful electric-blue dress
laid out upon the bed. It was of a rather peculiar shade, but
it was exceedingly rich and costly. It fitted me very well,
though it was evident that it had been made for someone taller
than myself. I put it on, and then, as instructed, I went down
stairs. Both Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle were waiting for me. They
seemed more than usually excited.

"'Now, Miss Hunter,' said Mr. Rucastle, 'will you be so very
kind as to go up to the attic?  There is a picture which my wife
wishes to have brought down.  Bring it down very carefully, as
it is extremely valuable.  I will show you the exact room.'

He led me upstairs himself.

"I went to my room and found the dress laid out as he had
stated. It was of a peculiar shade, a sort of bright electric
blue, such as I have never seen before. It was of a soft, silky
material, and the lining was of the finest and thinnest French
cambric. It was beautifully made, and I could see that it was a
very expensive garment. It was much too large for me, but I put
it on as I was directed and then went down to breakfast. Mr.
Rucastle was standing before the fire talking to his wife. He
turned round as I entered.

"'Capital!' he cried. 'It is a decided success. I knew it would
suit you. The shade is an important point. Now, I have a further
request, Miss Hunter.'

"'What is that, sir?' I asked.

"'It would be more convenient to us,' said he, 'if you were to
sleep in this room. It is the only spare one we have, and it is
near the nursery, so that you will hear the child if he wants
anything. I trust that there is nothing which you would object to
in this.'

"I had no reason to object, so I agreed at once."

"I went to my room and found the dress laid out as he had
described. It was of a peculiar shade, a sort of bright vivid
blue, such as I have never seen before. The material was soft
and thick, and it was made up in the most perfect manner. As I
put it on I could not help admiring myself in the glass. It was
certainly very becoming. It was quite unlike anything that I
had ever worn before. It was as different from my usual style as
possible, and I dare say it would suit me very well."

"It is clearly a question of dress rather than of morals that has
driven you to consult us," Holmes remarked dryly.

"You will soon find that I have other troubles besides those
connected with my clothes," said the young lady with some
dignity.

"The dress which I found waiting for me was of a peculiar shade
of blue. It was of excellent material, a sort of beige, but it
bore unmistakable signs of having been worn before. It could not
have been a better fit if I had been measured for it. Both Mr.
and Mrs. Rucastle expressed a delight at the look of it, which
seemed quite exaggerated in its vehemence. They were waiting for
me in the drawing-room, which is a very large room, stretching
along the entire front of the house, with three long windows
reaching down to the floor. A chair had been placed close to the
central window, with its back turned towards it. In this I was
asked to sit, and then Mr. Rucastle, walking up and down on the
other side of the room, began to tell me a series of the funniest
stories that I have ever listened to. You cannot imagine how
comical he was, and I laughed until I was quite weary. Mrs.
Rucastle, however, who has evidently no sense of humour, never so
much as smiled, but sat with her hands in her lap, and a sad,
anxious look upon her face. After an hour or so, Mr. Rucastle
suddenly remarked that it was time to commence the duties of the
day, and that I might change my dress and go to little Edward in
the nursery.

"This happened again and again. It was always the same. I was
placed in the same chair, I was given the same book to read, and
at the same point I was ordered to stop and to change my dress.
It was a most singular proceeding, Mr. Holmes, but at first I
could see nothing in it to excite my alarm. It was foolish and
frivolous, but not immoral. But then, day by day, as the same
thing continued, a very serious suspicion began to creep into my
mind, which was strengthened by the fact that several times when
I had been reading aloud I had observed a shadow which seemed to
me to be very much like that of a man, on the window-pane. I have
no doubt that it was only my fancy.

"Then another incident occurred to make me feel uneasy. You know
how very nervous I am of mice. I had observed that several times
my room had been overrun with mice during the night and this made
me feel nervous."

"This was the third time that the same thing had occurred. I had
begun to feel a little uneasy, and yet I could not imagine
anything to account for such singular conduct. The whole thing was
so utterly senseless and purposeless. I was beginning to think
that I was myself in some way the object of a practical joke,
when suddenly the explanation flashed upon me. I looked back at
the chair in which I had been sitting, and the very thought made
me shiver. If I had only remained seated for another few minutes,
it would have been too late! My hair would have been cut short
indeed!

"This happened several times. I began to feel a little uneasy,
as you may imagine, at the persistent recurrence of such a curious
incident. The only possible explanation which I could think of
was that it was some sort of game which they played for their
amusement, or perhaps it was some sort of a test of my powers of
observation. But, whatever it may be, it is very odd, and I can
assure you that it was not easy to sit there in the electric-blue
dress in a very bright light with a man walking up and down
looking at me as I read."

"It is certainly very peculiar," remarked Holmes.  "Was there
anything else at all unusual?"

"Yes," said Miss Hunter; "there was one other occurrence which
had the effect of completely puzzling me."

"This happened several times. I am sure that there was some
purpose behind it all, but what that purpose was I could not
imagine. There was nothing which I could see to guide me in
forming an opinion. It was quite clear to me, however, that the
whole thing was a sort of ritual with them, and that the more I
tried to fathom its meaning the more I should be baffled."

"But surely you asked them what it all meant?"

"I did, of course, on several occasions, but they always laughed
at my questions, and answered with some vague allusion to
'their little ways,' and 'the peculiarity of their dispositions.'
The whole thing is so strange that I cannot understand it. But now
my own story must take a more serious turn."

"This happened several times. I could not understand it. It
seemed to me that it must be some kind of a game or jest, but
neither Mr. nor Mrs. Rucastle ever alluded to it, and I could
not see anything in the room to explain it. I could not even
formulate any conjecture, Mr. Holmes, for there was no conceivable
reason for it."

"Let me see," said Holmes, stroking his chin thoughtfully. "You
sat in a chair with your back to the window. It was a bright
sunny day. You changed your dress twice. What was it like?"

"The electric-blue dress, sir. You see it would have been
unsuitable in the nursery."

"And how about this strange conduct? What is your own opinion of
it all?"

"My opinion, sir, is that Mrs. Rucastle is a very strange
woman, and that her husband is also peculiar. I have been
constantly uneasy. To-day, however, things have come to a climax
which made me determine to appeal to you at once."

"Pray relate your experiences."

"You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how curious I became as to
what the meaning of this extraordinary performance could possibly
be. They were always very careful, I observed, to turn my face
away from the window, so that I became consumed with the desire
to see what was going on behind my back. At first it seemed to be
impossible, but I soon devised a means. My hand-mirror had been
broken, so a happy thought seized me, and I concealed a piece of
the glass in my handkerchief. On the next occasion, in the midst
of my laughter, I put my handkerchief up to my eyes, and was able
with a little management to see all that there was behind me. I
confess that I was disappointed. There was nothing. At least that
was my first impression. At the second glance, however, I
perceived that there was a man standing in the Southampton Road,
a small bearded man in a grey suit, who seemed to be looking in
my direction. The road is an important highway, and there are
usually people there. This man, however, was leaning against the
railings which bordered our field and was looking earnestly up. I
lowered my handkerchief and glanced at Mrs. Rucastle to find her
eyes fixed upon me with a most searching gaze. She said nothing,
but I am convinced that she had divined that I had a mirror in my
hand and had seen what was behind me. She rose at once.

"'Jephro,' said she, 'there is an impertinent fellow upon the
road there who stares up at Miss Hunter.'

"'No friend of yours, Miss Hunter?' he asked.

"'No, I know no one in these parts.'

"'Dear me! How very impertinent! Kindly turn round and motion to
him to go away.'

"'Surely it would be better to take no notice.'

"'No, no, we should have him loitering here always. Kindly turn
round and wave him away like that.'

"Since then, my life has been quite uneventful. I have my duties
with the child, and I sit in the nursery, or walk in the grounds.
The only strange thing is that my employer seems to have changed
his manner towards me. He is still kind, but there is a
nervousness in his manner which was not there before. He is
constantly looking over his shoulder, and if he sees anyone
approaching he immediately brings the conversation to an end. His
wife, on the other hand, is more amiable, or perhaps it would be
more accurate to say, that her manner has lost that pathetic
sadness which it formerly exhibited. She seems to be quite
cheerful now, and is quite attentive to me, and very desirous
that I should be happy in my new situation.

"But I am not happy. I cannot understand the meaning of my
employer's altered manner. He is not afraid of me. I cannot help
thinking that this man in the road must have some connexion with
the affairs of the house, and the fact that he seems to have
disappeared is very curious. It is this, Mr. Holmes, which has
made me anxious and made me determine to come to you for advice."

"And you did quite right," said Holmes. "You have observed keenly
and reasoned logically, though it must be confessed that the
mystery is a deep one. But we have already made some progress
towards its solution, and I shall have no difficulty in proving
to you that your instincts have not betrayed you, and that the
man upon the road is undoubtedly connected with the events which
have occurred at the Copper Beeches."

"There is not much more to tell. I am treated very kindly, but
I am kept a prisoner in the house. I have no means of leaving,
and they even seem to take my letters and my telegrams. It was
only by a lucky chance that I managed to get rid of Toller for a
few moments this morning, and slip into Winchester to send you
this message. My life is a complete mystery to me, Mr. Holmes. I
have no idea what they want, or what their motives can be. Why
should they make me sit in that window in that dress? Why should
they keep my letters and telegrams? And who is the man in the
grey suit?"

"It is a most singular business," said Holmes, thoughtfully.  "It
has certainly some points of interest. What is the nature of the
house? Do you mean that you have not been allowed to walk in the
garden?"

"Oh, yes, I have walked in the grounds, but they are very small,
and the doors of the house are locked, and Toller is always with
me."

"And Toller's wife?"

"I see little of her."

"Does Mr. Rucastle give you many orders?"

"No, he has been quite kind, but it is Mrs. Rucastle who has
been so strict."

"Does she give you any explanation of all this?"

"None."

"And your letters are taken?"

"Yes, or else sent unopened."

"Have you any idea who takes them?"

"I don't know. I think it may be Mrs. Toller."

"Tell me exactly how you have occupied your time during your
stay."

"I have spent a good deal of time in reading novels, and in
thinking over this strange experience."

"And what do you make of it?"

"It is all such a mystery, but it is bound to mean something.
Sometimes I have thought that it might be an affair of blackmail.
You know they must know something about me which they want to
conceal. Or else it is a matter of some plot which is being
managed from outside the house, and it is I who am the innocent
victim. But who is the man, and who is his employer? And what
is his design?"

Holmes remained silent for some time, stroking his chin thoughtfully.

"The mystery grows," he said finally. "But it is not insoluble.
We have certain clues: the mystery of the dress, the mystery of
the window and the man, and the mystery of the intercepted
letters. We must attack each one of these in turn, and make our
way towards the center of the problem."


"Well, Mr. Holmes, from that day things have gone on much as
usual, except that I have had more time to think over this
strange incident. It has made me very uneasy. The behaviour of
Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle is so strange, their servants are so
disagreeable, the child is so terrible, and the position of the
house is so lonely that I have come to the conclusion that I
cannot remain longer here. I had a letter this morning from the
agency telling me that they had a vacancy for a nursery governess
in a situation near Highgate which would suit me admirably. I
have written to accept it, and am leaving to-morrow. I should
never have thought of leaving without consulting you, Mr. Holmes,
had it not been for the urgent need of money and the fear of
making myself permanently liable to some curious persecution,
though I can form no notion as to what that persecution might be."

"You have done very wisely," remarked Holmes, pushing back his
chair and lighting a cigarette. "I would not have you remain
another day in that house if you could get away. Your narrative
certainly presents several singular points. The behaviour of your
employer is quite inexplicable; and the incident of the man in
the road is certainly puzzling."

"Is he not someone connected with your past, Mr. Holmes?"

"I am not likely to have enemies in such unlikely parts of
Hampshire. The affair is clearly connected with the other facts
which we have already discussed, and it may even lead us to the
very end of the mystery which we are now about to explore."

"But what is the mystery, Mr. Holmes?"

"We have only a very vague idea at present; but some further
data may possibly give us more accurate conclusions."

"Do you think there is some danger?"

"I am not sure, but I think it is very likely that you have
fallen into some unpleasant complication which would be better
avoided. I am only surprised that they did not make you go through
the performance once more before you left."

"No doubt they would have done so, but I had already written for
the Highgate post."

"You have done well. The telegram which you sent me was certainly
timely. I think that if we drive out to the Copper Beeches this
afternoon we may be able to clear up some points in this strange
business."

"There is not very much more to tell. From that day on, my life
became even more monotonous than before. I spent my mornings with
young Edward, who, as I have already explained, was a most
unpleasant and trying child. In the afternoons I had a little
reading, or I would wander about the grounds. The servants were
as silent and as surly as ever, but I saw nothing more of the man
in the road. The weather was fine, and I took the opportunity
after lunch of having a walk in the grounds. As I passed the
copper beeches, I observed that several of the lower branches
had been bent down and fastened with strong cord. As they had
been rather carefully concealed among the other branches I could
hardly believe that it was merely accidental. A sudden thought
then occurred to me. I had been told that the copper beeches
overshadowed the road, and I had already observed that it was from
the direction of the road that the man had appeared. The
arrangement of the branches would make an excellent hiding-place
for a person who desired to lie concealed. This fact, with the
obvious desire to have my back turned towards this place, made me
conclude that there must be something amiss in that direction. I
returned to the house, and when I was alone I tried to make some
inquiries from Toller.

"I began by asking him some questions about the estate, but I
could get nothing out of him except grunts and snarls. At last I
asked him plainly whether there had been any persons in hiding
among the copper beeches. He turned pale, and for a moment I
thought he was going to strike me.

"'None as I knows on,' said he, 'but if there was, what's your
business with it?'

"'I shall report you to your master if you answer me in such a
fashion,' I retorted.

"'Report me, would ye? I'll report ye, first, if you don't mind
it. And it's the best report that ye'll ever have. He would be
the most dangerous man in this house if you upset him.' Then he
turned and slouched out of the room, leaving me to imagine what he
meant.

"There is not much more to tell.  Yesterday morning, however,
Mr. Rucastle came into my room and asked me to come down into the
drawing-room, as he wished to speak to me.  When I got there I
found his wife dressed and ready for her walk, but Mr. Rucastle
himself was in his dressing-gown.  He said to me, quite
casually, that he was sorry that he had to leave home for some
days, and that I must be careful to obey his wife’s instructions
during his absence.  She gave me a few orders in her usual
listless manner, and then they went out together.  As soon as
they were gone, I began to think what I should do; and finally
I decided to get away for a day and come and consult you before I
returned.  There is something so strange about it all, Mr. Holmes,
that my mind is quite upset by it.  It was for that reason that I
sent for you."

"And your telegram made no mention of this gentleman in the grey
suit?" asked Holmes.

"No, sir.  I only wished you to come and see the matter for
yourself."

"You will find it rather disconnected, I fear, and there may
prove to be little relation between the different incidents of
which I speak. On the very first day that I was at the Copper
Beeches, Mr. Rucastle took me to a small outhouse which stands
near the kitchen door. As we approached it I heard the sharp
rattling of a chain, and the sound as of a large animal moving
about.

"'Look in here!' said Mr. Rucastle, showing me a slit between two
planks. 'Is he not a beauty?'

"I looked through and was conscious of two glowing eyes, and of a
vague figure huddled up in the darkness.

"I thanked him for his warning, and, indeed, I had no wish to
make a closer acquaintance with such a formidable guardian. But
the incident is, as far as I can judge, entirely unconnected
with the other events which I have described. It is only now,
when I have been asked to give my narrative to you, that I see
how curiously they are linked together."

"Indeed, it is most strange," said Holmes. "Pray proceed."

"That same evening I heard a most fearful yell, which seemed to
come from the very heart of the house. It sent a shiver down my
spine. I was sitting alone in the nursery at the time, and the
only other person near was Mrs. Toller, the housemaid, who was
busy making up the fire in the next room. I asked her what it
was, but she would only shake her head and said that there were
strange noises at night. A few minutes later I heard the same
cry, and then all was silent. Next morning at breakfast I
mentioned the sounds which I had heard during the night, but the
others seemed to think little of it. Mr. Rucastle said that it
was probably some dog barking in the neighbourhood, and Mrs.
Rucastle showed just that same curious look of anxiety which I
have already mentioned."

"That was all he said, but the incident made a great impression
upon my mind. The dog seemed to me to be unusually large and
fierce, and I could not help wondering whether it had ever been
trained to attack. The next day I saw the man Toller drunk and
bullying his wife. She was very quiet, but I could read the
resentment in her eyes. That night I heard the chain rattle again
as I went to my room. The thought of the fierce dog made me very
nervous, and I bolted my door and put a chair against it before I
went to bed. However, I slept soundly enough."

"You have done well," said Holmes. "Continue, please."


"That was all he said, but the incident impressed itself upon
my mind, and I have several times since thought of the creature
and wondered whether it was really so ferocious as my employer
would have me believe. I have never seen him, but I have heard
him at night, growling and howling. It is a most dreadful sound,
and I cannot describe the nervous strain of hearing it every
night. One would think that such a thing would become a matter of
custom, but no, I am no nearer to it now than I was a week ago. I
can never become accustomed to that noise. Last night I heard
something else. After the growling had subsided, which it did
about midnight, I heard a low, soft scratching at my window. I
tried to sleep, but I could not. There was also the continual
noise of some one walking heavily in the room above mine. Then
came the scratching again. I can only describe the noise as the
scratching of a rat's claws, and as this was going on in the same
spot night after night it was impossible for me to doubt that the
animal was endeavouring to gain admission to my room. I could
imagine what it would feel like to be seized by that fearful
creature, and I feel sure that such a night's experience would
make me incapable of any further duties in the house. That is why
I came to you, Mr. Holmes."

"That was the first I heard of the ferocious Carlo. Since then I
have seen him several times, sometimes during the day, but always
from a distance. He is a magnificent beast, a tawny yellow
mastiff, with a black muzzle, and enormous jaws. He is kept in a
small kennel which is just outside the kitchen door. It is quite
plain to me that the man in the road is a friend of Toller's,
and that they both have designs upon the house. I dare not go
further without advice."

"But what are their designs?"

"I cannot imagine. Mr. Rucastle has been quite kind to me. It
might be a robbery, or it might be something far more serious.
One night I heard a strange cry outside my window. I opened the
curtains and looked out. There was a dark figure against the
background of the lighted room which was just behind me. I pulled
the curtain down again, but from the sound of his footsteps I
could tell that the man was going round and round the house,
evidently trying every window and door. I could not tell what he
wanted, nor could I have said who he was, for the night was very
dark.

"I was so alarmed that I crept to Mrs. Rucastle's room, and
explained to her what had happened. She listened patiently, but
when I had concluded my story she made no remark at all, but
pointed with her finger to a small door on the farther side of
the room.

"'You can go into that room,' said she; 'and sleep there, as it
is all empty. I can better spare my own.'

"I took her advice, and have slept there ever since."

"It was very kind of her," remarked Holmes.

"Well, I'm not so sure about the kindness. It seemed to me then
that she was trying to get rid of me somehow. The other night
something happened which made me dreadfully anxious, for my fears
became centred on Mr. Rucastle. I was in my bedroom about ten
o'clock when I heard a knock at the door."

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was silvered over and almost as bright as day. I was
standing, rapt in the peaceful beauty of the scene, when I was
aware that something was moving under the shadow of the copper
beeches. As it emerged into the moonshine I saw what it was. It
was a giant dog, as large as a calf, tawny tinted, with hanging
jowl, black muzzle, and huge projecting bones. It walked slowly
across the lawn and vanished into the shadow upon the other side.
That dreadful sentinel sent a chill to my heart which I do not
think that any burglar could have done.

"My hair had been cut off, as I have told you, in London. I had
put it in my trunk, and I had never seen it since. How could it
have got into that drawer? I assure you that my hair stood on
end when I saw it lying there. It seemed to me that there must be
someone in the house who had a secret interest in my actions,
someone who was playing a game with me. I took the hair out,
placed it back in my trunk, and locked the drawer again. But I
could not shake off the impression that something was seriously
wrong."

"Well, Miss Hunter, it certainly does seem a queer business,"
remarked Holmes.

"And now, Mr. Holmes, I want your advice as to what I should do.
I do not like my surroundings. I feel that I am watched and
followed. I am nervous and irritable. I wish to leave."

"I think you're quite right. You should leave."

"I took it out and examined it carefully. It was undoubtedly my
own hair, but it had been very cleverly treated. It had been
singed and scorched in several places, so that it was of a
uniform dull greyish colour, and the ends were curled and frizzled
to conceal the fact that it had been cut off recently. It was
quite clear that it had been put there, and it seemed equally
clear that someone had been trying to do away with it. I placed it
back in the drawer, closed it, and locked it. Then I went to bed,
but I slept badly, for I felt uneasy about the matter."

"I took it up and examined it carefully. It was undoubtedly my
own hair, but it was very dusty and the ends were yellow and
frazzled as if it had been roughly used. It had certainly been
put back in the drawer, but it was not I who had put it there.
The incident made me uneasy, and I felt that there was something
about the whole place that was not quite right.

"And now, Mr. Holmes, I want your advice. What am I to do?"

"I took it out and examined it carefully. It was undoubtedly my
own hair, but it was matted and discoloured, as though it had been
pulled violently from its fastenings. It was quite damp, too, as
though it had been recently taken out of water. I was very
much puzzled, and stared at it in astonishment. Then I locked the
drawer again and put away my keys, and I went to bed, and slept
as soundly as I could after such a curious experience.


"I took it up, and looked at it, and then I looked round the room.
There could be no doubt that it was my own hair, but it had been
very cleverly fastened together again at the end, and it looked
as though it had never been touched. I replaced it in the drawer
and locked it up, for I was beginning to feel rather frightened.
I went to bed, but I had little sleep, and I did not dare to look
out of my window lest the dog should be prowling about once more
under the copper beeches. In the morning I looked for my hair, but
it was gone. In its place were two letters, which had evidently
been placed there before I had taken away the hair."

"What did the letters contain?" asked Holmes eagerly.

"I took it up and examined it. It was of the same peculiar tint,
and the same thickness. But then the impossibility of the thing
obtruded itself upon me. How could my hair have been locked in
the drawer? With trembling hands I undid my trunk, turned out the
contents, and drew from the bottom my own hair. I laid the two
tresses together, and I assure you that they were identical. Was
it not extraordinary? Puzzle as I would, I could make nothing at
all of what it meant. I returned the strange hair to the drawer,
and I said nothing of the matter to the Rucastles as I felt that
I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer which they had
locked.

"That same evening, as I was sitting with Mrs. Rucastle, she
suddenly started up with an exclamation of horror. Her eyes were
fixed upon the window, and her face was as white as death.
'There he is!' she cried, 'there he is!' I looked, but I could
see no one. She sank back into her chair, trembling all over, and
she whispered to me, 'That man, Miss Hunter, is my brother. He
has been here before. He is mad, and if he finds me here I am
lost. I have been away from home for several years, and he has
been hunting me all the time. If he finds me, he will murder me,
for he has threatened it often. I have changed my name and have
lived under an assumed one, that he might not trace me. I only
trust that he does not know my new name. I dare not go to
Winchester, for I fear that he would find me.'

"That same evening, as I was sitting in the window, I saw Toller
the groom coming stealthily out of this room, with a lighted
lantern in his hand. He walked quickly across the lawn towards
the woods, and I, fearing that some mischief was afoot, followed
him at a distance, keeping under the shadow of the trees. I
watched him, and as he was about to enter the wood, a man
emerged from the darkness and seized him by the throat. They
struggled for a moment, and then the man, who seemed to be the
stronger of the two, disarmed the groom and plunged him, with his
face downwards, into a deep pool which lies under the branches of
a great oak. I watched until he had dragged him into the centre
of the pool. Then he came back for the lantern, which he threw
into the pool after him, and then, with the same stealthy tread
which he had shown before, he returned, making his way back to
the house. I never saw his face, nor can I tell his height, but I
can tell that he was large and muscular, and that he had a very
high-pitched voice. This was the end of my strange experiences at
the Copper Beeches."

"A most extraordinary story," said Holmes, with a slight smile,
"and one which certainly does not tend to increase one's
confidence in the domestic arrangements of Mr. Jephro Rucastle.
What conclusions have you yourself drawn?"

"I was keenly interested, and I made up my mind that I would
discover what was in that room. I had no particular reason for
thinking that anything dreadful was there; it was simply my
natural curiosity, which, I confess, is very strong. That same
evening, while the family were at supper, I took a small bunch of
keys which I had found in the passage, which I concluded to belong
to the house, and tried whether they would open the door. The
second key which I tried fitted exactly, and I found myself in
the room. It was large and bare, with only a single chair, a
table, and a great iron-bound chest in the center. It was the
chest which I had examined, and it was very heavy, but I thought
that perhaps I could move it by straining with my whole weight
upon it, and so, with my shoulder braced against it, and my
teeth gritted, I was pressing with my whole weight, when I heard
the door open behind me. I turned with a cry of alarm, and saw
Mr. Rucastle standing there.

"That same evening, as I was sitting in the nursery, I heard a
most dreadful scream from the direction of the locked wing. I
rushed out to the passage, but Mrs. Rucastle was already there
before me. Her face was ashen, her hands were clenched, and her
eyes were wide open with terror. She had a candle in her hand,
and she held it up to me, and then turned and led the way to the
wing. I heard a sound like the sobbing of a woman, but I was
afraid to go any farther, and I saw the Toller couple come out
of their quarters and stand looking after us with amazement.
Mrs. Rucastle was trembling in every limb, and I could see that
she was hardly able to stand. With an effort she managed to
unlock the door, and then we entered together into the room
from which the sound had come.

"That same evening, as I was sitting in the nursery, I heard a
most dreadful scream from the direction of the locked wing. It
was a woman's scream, and it was followed by a prolonged and
most agonizing groan. I rushed to the door, but it was locked, and
as I was turning away in despair I heard the key turning in the
lock. The door opened, and Mrs. Rucastle came out, her face as
white as death, her clothes torn, and a deep scratch upon her
cheek. She did not seem to see me, but passed on to her own
room, where I heard her fall upon her knees in prayer. I have
seen her several times since then with her face pale and her
dress torn; and I know that she has been very unhappy. To-day I
found an empty bottle of laudanum in the nursery, which I
concluded had been used by Mrs. Rucastle. I was alarmed for her
safety; but what could I do? I was bound by my engagement not to
leave the house. This was the state of affairs which caused me to
appeal to you by telegraph. My time here is up, and I must return
to the Copper Beeches by three o'clock."

"Then, my dear Miss Hunter," said Holmes, rising, "we must act at
once. And you are right. You cannot wait any longer. We must
take action."

"This aroused my curiosity, so when I went out for a walk in the
grounds with my charge, I strolled round to the side from which I
could see the windows of this part of the house. There were four
of them in a row, three of which were simply dirty, while the
fourth was shuttered up. They were evidently all deserted. As I
strolled up and down, glancing at them occasionally, Mr. Rucastle
came out to me, looking as merry and jovial as ever.

"'Ah!' said he, 'you must not think me rude if I passed you
without a word, my dear young lady. I was preoccupied with
business matters.'

"I assured him that I was not offended. 'By the way,' said I,
'you seem to have quite a suite of spare rooms up there, and one
of them has the shutters up.'

"He looked surprised and, as it seemed to me, a little startled
at my remark.

"That is all that I have to tell you, Mr. Holmes, except that
yesterday I saw something which seemed to me to be very
extraordinary. I was in the pantry, helping Mrs. Toller to
arrange the tea-things, when I observed that she was staring
hard at Mr. Rucastle who was seated by the kitchen fire. He was
cutting up a large fish, but his hand shook so that some of the
slices dropped into the saucer. 'What is the matter?' said I;
'does he not feel well?' Mrs. Toller said nothing, but she
watched him intently and shook her head sadly. When the
opportunity offered itself, I stepped into the passage and watched
him more closely. I saw that his hands trembled very much.

"That is all that I have to tell you."

"From that day forth I began to watch them more carefully, and
my suspicions grew into a certainty. There are two things which
are quite inexplicable to me, Mr. Holmes. First, why did they
take such pains to turn my face away from the window during the
two visits which I made to their drawing-room? And, second, what
was the reason for the return of my own hair to my room? It was
not Mrs. Rucastle who took it, for I have never left the room
during her presence. It was not Toller, for he never enters it.
It must, therefore, have been Mr. Rucastle, but what is the
meaning of it? It is a most inexplicable thing."

"Let us consider the first point," said Holmes.  "Why were you
turned away from the window?  What could be seen from it that
they wished to hide?"


"That evening, as I was sitting with Mrs. Rucastle, she suddenly
said to me, 'Do you know, Miss Hunter, that you have a very
remarkable resemblance to my husband's first wife?'

"I thanked her for the compliment, but said that I had never
heard that I bore any resemblance to anyone.

"'Oh, yes,' she said thoughtfully. 'I have a photograph of her
here somewhere. It was taken before her marriage. Perhaps I
could find it for you.'

"She rummaged in her drawer and produced a very fine photograph of
a most beautiful girl. The eyes were certainly very much like my
own, but I could see no other resemblance."

"From that time forward I have felt an uneasiness in my mind
which has culminated in my writing to you. There is something
very strange going on in that house, Mr. Holmes, and I wish that
I had never set foot in it. I feel sure that if I were to remain
longer I should become involved in something very serious. This
man, whoever he may be, who looks up at me from the road, this
locked wing, this strange duplicate hair, are all very puzzling
matters, and I cannot but feel that there is some mystery which
I should do well to leave to you to unravel."

"It is certainly a curious collection of incidents," remarked
Holmes. "But I must confess that I am unable at present to form
any opinion as to their bearing on each other. The one thing
which seems clear is that some one is interested in you. That is
the man whom you saw in the road."

"But why?"

"That is what we must find out."


"That same evening, as I was sitting with Mrs. Rucastle, she
suddenly asked me if I had seen anything of a dark-haired young
man upon the road. I said that I had seen no one but the man
whom she had described as impertinent.

"'Ah!' said she, 'that was not the one that I meant. The one I
mean has dark hair and a dark mustache. He walks with a slight
limp, and is taller than the other one.'

"I said that I had seen no such person. She smiled in a strange,
knowing way and said no more. But from that time I observed that
she always looked at me with a curious expression, as if she
were trying to read my thoughts.

"Well, Mr. Holmes, from the moment that I understood that there
was something about that suite of rooms which I was not to know,
I was all on fire to go over them. It was not mere curiosity,
though I have my share of that. It was more a feeling of duty--a
feeling that some good might come from my penetrating to this
place. They talk of woman's instinct; perhaps it was woman's
instinct which gave me that feeling. At any rate, it was there,
and I was keenly on the lookout for any chance to pass the
forbidden door.

"There were three rooms, all in a row. The first was a large one,
with a dusty, worn carpet, and several chairs and tables covered
with papers and photographs. The second was smaller, with a
window looking out into the Southampton Road, and it was in this
that I saw the man whom I had observed on the previous occasions.
He was looking up at the window, and, as it happened, the shutter
was open. He was a small, dark, sharp-faced man, with a cruel
look about his eyes, and a thin, cruel mouth. He had a small
pointed beard and wore a dark grey suit. I saw him perfectly, for
the moment, and should know him again anywhere. I was so
absorbed in watching him that I did not at first observe that
anyone was in the third room.

"The suite consisted of three rooms, all of them very dusty and
in disorder, but furnished in a style which showed that they had
once been occupied by a person of refinement. There were water-
colours on the walls, Persian rugs upon the floor, and handsome
curtains hanging from the windows. In the second room, however,
which was smaller than the others, I found something which
startled me so that I have hardly recovered from my surprise yet.

"It was a woman's room. A lady's silk dressing-gown was hung
upon the wall, and several articles of feminine apparel lay upon
the dressing-table. But it was not that which moved me. It was
the fact that I found my own hair there.

"It was done up in the same coil which I had taken from my trunk
that evening, and it was unmistakably mine. It was I, and I alone,
who had done it up in that way. How could it be here?"

"The mystery deepens," said Holmes. "This is most extraordinary.
Pray continue."

"The suite consists of three rooms, all of which were unfurnished,
except for a few odds and ends of lumber. The windows were all
locked and shuttered, so that it was very dark inside, but I
managed to find my way into the third room. There I saw a sight
which I shall never forget. There was an old-fashioned bureau
against the wall, and above it hung a mirror. In the bureau was
a single key, and upon the glass of the mirror a single blood-red
fingerprint."

"The suite consisted of two rooms, a sitting-room and a bedroom.
The sitting-room was dusty and disordered, with papers and
photographic apparatus scattered on the floor. The bedroom was
empty except for a large wooden chest in one corner. It was locked,
but after trying several keys I found one which fitted, and opened
it. Inside there was a pile of clothes and some jewelry, and,
lying on top of all, a small black notebook bound with leather.

"You will scarcely believe, Mr. Holmes, what I found written in
this little book. It was a record of Mr. Rucastle's misdeeds,
written, so far as I can judge, in the hand of his first wife. It
was a ghastly tale of bigamy, cruelty, and violence, the whole
record of a terrible life. But it was not this which interested
me most, as much as the last entry in the book. This was written
in a different ink and in another hand, and these were the words:

"The suite consisted of three rooms, all unfurnished and bare,
except for a few broken chairs and some empty packing-cases. The
windows of two of them were dark, but the third, which faced the
grounds, had its shutters open, and through this I could see
that it was a large room with several cupboards let into the
walls. One of these stood open, and I saw that it contained a
large number of old magazines, some of them bound, others loose,
and other things, the nature of which I did not see. I took the
opportunity of glancing round, but there was nothing else of any
interest in the room. As I turned to go I heard the sound of
footsteps below, and at once I realized that it was time to go. I
shut the door, replaced the key, and returned to my room without
any one having observed my absence."


"There was a little passage in front of me, unpapered and
uncarpeted, which turned at a right angle at the farther end.
Round this corner were three doors in a line, the first and third
of which were open. They each led into an empty room, dusty and
cheerless, with two windows in the one and one in the other, so
thick with dirt that the evening light glimmered dimly through
them. The centre door was closed, and across the outside of it
had been fastened one of the broad bars of an iron bed, padlocked
at one end to a ring in the wall, and fastened at the other with
stout cord. The door itself was locked as well, and the key was
not there. This barricaded door corresponded clearly with the
shuttered window outside, and yet I could see by the glimmer from
beneath it that the room was not in darkness. Evidently there was
a skylight which let in light from above. As I stood in the
passage gazing at the sinister door and wondering what secret it
might veil, I suddenly heard the sound of steps within the room
and saw a shadow pass backward and forward against the little
slit of dim light which shone out from under the door. A mad,
unreasoning terror rose up in me at the sight, Mr. Holmes. My
overstrung nerves failed me suddenly, and I turned and ran--ran
as though some dreadful hand were behind me clutching at the
skirt of my dress. I rushed down the passage, through the door,
and straight into the arms of Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting
outside.

"'So,' said he, smiling, 'it was you, then. I thought that it
must be when I saw the door open.'

"'Oh, I am so frightened!' I panted.

"'My dear young lady! my dear young lady!'--you cannot think how
caressing and soothing his manner was--'and what has frightened
you, my dear young lady?'

"But his voice was just a little too coaxing. He overdid it. I
was keenly on my guard against him.

"'I was foolish enough to go into the empty wing,' I answered.
'But it is so lonely and eerie in this dim light that I was
frightened and ran out again. Oh, it is so dreadfully still in
there!'

"'Only that?' said he, looking at me keenly.

"'Why, what did you think?' I asked.

"'Why do you think that I lock this door?'

"'I am sure that I do not know.'

"'It is to keep people out who have no business there. Do you
see?' He was still smiling in the most amiable manner.

"'I am sure if I had known--'

"I understood then that I had been within an ace of discovering
some dreadful secret. I felt that my life was not safe while I
remained under the roof of that man, and I resolved to leave
next day. But before I did so I determined to find out what that
dark room contained.

"He actually shook his fist in my face as he spoke, and I could
see that he was capable of carrying out his threat. I was so
terrified that I could hardly stand. I felt that there was some
dark secret about that room which must never be revealed, and I
was glad to get away with my life. I slipped back to my own
quarters, and since then I have not ventured out at night, though
I confess that I feel sometimes as though I should never know
peace until I have found out what it is that they keep locked up
in that room."

"This is certainly a very curious and interesting situation,"
remarked Holmes. "I confess that I am very much interested, and
I should very much like to see this room for myself. That,
however, is not a matter for immediate action. We must take
things as they come and act upon our best judgment at each stage.
What have you done, Miss Hunter, since this incident?"

"He actually shook his fist in my face as he spoke, and I could
see that he was capable of carrying out his threat. I was
horrified at his violence, and I could only stammer out that I
would never do it again. 'Very well, then,' said he; 'remember
what I have said. Go down to your tea. I am sure you are
nervous and upset.' And with a parting assurance that I was to
confine myself to my own quarters, he left me to my own
reflections."

"I understood then that I had to deal with a man who was
capable of anything.  I felt that my only safety lay in getting
away from the Copper Beeches, and that was why I telegraphed to
you.  I had promised Mr. Rucastle to be back by three, so I
hurried down.  I am so thankful that you have come.  What am I
to do?"  She looked up at Holmes with appealing eyes.

"He seized me by the arm and shook me fiercely.  I was so terrified
that I could hardly stand.  He released me at last, and I fled to
my room, and have not left it since, except to come down to meet
you. I have had food sent up to my room, and, except for the
servants, I have seen no one.  I am determined not to go back to
that house again."


"I was so terrified that I do not know what I did. I suppose that
I must have rushed past him into my room. I remember nothing
until I found myself lying on my bed trembling all over. Then I
thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not live there longer without
some advice. I was frightened of the house, of the man, of the
woman, of the servants, even of the child. They were all horrible
to me. If I could only bring you down all would be well. Of
course I might have fled from the house, but my curiosity was
almost as strong as my fears. My mind was soon made up. I would
send you a wire. I put on my hat and cloak, went down to the
office, which is about half a mile from the house, and then
returned, feeling very much easier. A horrible doubt came into my
mind as I approached the door lest the dog might be loose, but I
remembered that Toller had drunk himself into a state of
insensibility that evening, and I knew that he was the only one
in the household who had any influence with the savage creature,
or who would venture to set him free. I slipped in in safety and
lay awake half the night in my joy at the thought of seeing you.
I had no difficulty in getting leave to come into Winchester this
morning, but I must be back before three o'clock, for Mr. and
Mrs. Rucastle are going on a visit, and will be away all the
evening, so that I must look after the child. Now I have told you
all my adventures, Mr. Holmes, and I should be very glad if you
could tell me what it all means, and, above all, what I should
do."

"Excellent! We shall have time to make a little investigation
before we start for the Copper Beeches. I am of opinion, Watson,
that the situation is more serious than you imagine. I have,
however, a plan." He then outlined his plan to me, adding, "It is
a risky one, and may even prove to be dangerous, but it is our
only chance of getting at the truth.  This is no mere matter of a
whimsical household; there is something far more sinister at work
here, and it is our duty to bring it to light.  We must be
quick, and above all, we must be careful. The least mistake may
have terrible consequences."

"Excellent! Then we have everything that we need. Watson, I think

This is a most singular and fascinating problem, and the solution
is, I fancy, one which may lie very close at hand. In the
meantime, Miss Hunter, let us have some more of this excellent
lunch, and then we can discuss what we are to do. I think that
a little trip to this place which you so vividly describe will
clear up all our difficulties."

"Excellent. Then we shall require no more information. Miss
Hunter, you have done remarkably well. You have shown some
initiative and resource in making the journey down here alone, and
have gained some very interesting information. But I think that
we must now proceed to the Copper Beeches and bring this matter
to a conclusion. I confess that it is rather a curious and
complicated little problem. It is, however, quite within our
powers to unravel it, and we shall do so by bringing all our
energies to bear upon it. Toller, you say, is drunk; the Rucastles
are away, and you are left in charge of the child. I am afraid
that you must be prepared for some very unpleasant developments,
but the end may be worth the means."

"Excellent! Then we shall have time to look round the house
before we return to London. As to your own situation, Miss
Hunter, I would advise you to do nothing at all for the present.
Leave everything as it is, and we shall soon see our way. Now let
us have a look at this curious place which seems to be the centre
of so much mystery."

"And the dog, Carlo? Is he chained up?"

"Yes, always during the day."

"Excellent," said Holmes. "Then we will proceed to the Copper
Beeches at once. It is a most interesting case, and I shall
congratulate you, Miss Hunter, on having had the good sense to
choose this particular crisis to send for me. Your observation
has been admirable."

"It is all due to your teaching, Mr. Holmes," she answered
eagerly. "I have learned so much from your books."

"You are an apt pupil," said he with a smile. "Now we shall soon
get to the bottom of this mystery."

"You seem to me to have acted all through this matter like a very
brave and sensible girl, Miss Hunter. Do you think that you could
perform one more feat? I should not ask it of you if I did not
think you a quite exceptional woman."

"I will try. What is it?"

"Excellent! Then we shall have a clear field. We shall be able to
examine the mysterious suite of rooms, and perhaps discover the
secret which they contain. You may leave the rest to us. And
now," he added, glancing at his watch, "it is time that we
started for the Copper Beeches.  We must be there by seven."

"Excellent! I am sure that we shall find something interesting
in that room which is kept so carefully locked. Now, let us have
some lunch, and then we will make our preparations. You must leave
us to arrange our plans, but we may depend upon your co-operation
when the time comes."

"Excellent! Then, when we arrive, we shall find everything
prepared for us. You will have your reward. There is a certain
mystery about this house which will probably never be cleared up
unless we can bring the culprits to book. It is my belief that
we have here a case of extraordinary interest, which may have
far-reaching consequences. And now let us go."

We left the hotel together, and at the appointed time we were
driving towards the Copper Beeches.

"Excellent! We shall then have a free hand. Now, let us look at
the situation. You have seen a man looking at the house. You have
found your own hair in a drawer. You have seen that the servants
have been tampering with that wing of the house which is locked.
There is something mysterious about the locked room itself, and
your employer has shown some anxiety as to whether you should
enter it. There is a dog of immense size and ferocity on the
premises. Finally, the unusual salary and the odd conditions
which were made when you were engaged."

"Excellent! Then you shall have my warmest congratulations. I
think that you will find that you have done more good in this
house than you would have done in a dozen schools. Now let us
consider what is to be done. It is clear that there is something
wrong here, and it is our duty to find out what it is. I fancy
that we shall find our clue in that locked room."

"Yes, but who is there to unlock the door?"

"Perhaps we shall find the key."

"But the padlock?"

"A strong pair of pincers should deal with that."

"And the dog?"

"The groom is drunk, remember?"

"Well, we are prepared for any emergency. Let us go."

"Excellent! We shall then look thoroughly into the affair. Of
course there is only one feasible explanation. You have been
brought there to personate someone, and the real person is
imprisoned in this chamber. That is obvious. As to who this
prisoner is, I have no doubt that it is the daughter, Miss Alice

America. You were chosen, doubtless, as resembling her in height,
figure, and the colour of your hair. Hers had been cut off, very
possibly in some illness through which she has passed, and so, of
course, yours had to be sacrificed also. By a curious chance you
came upon her tresses. The man in the road was undoubtedly some
friend of hers--possibly her fiancé--and no doubt, as you wore

laughter, whenever he saw you, and afterwards from your gesture,

clear. The most serious point in the case is the disposition of
the child."

"What on earth has that to do with it?" I ejaculated.

"But what can we do?"

"We shall see when we get there. But one thing is certain: we
must act, and act quickly."  Holmes sprang to his feet as he
spoke, and a few minutes later we were both in a hansom, driving
as fast as we could to Waterloo Station to catch the express for
Winchester.

"But what are we to do?"

"We shall go to the Copper Beeches to-night, and we shall
liberate Miss Rucastle.  It is a most interesting problem,
Watson, and one which presents more than one curious feature."

"But what can we do?"

"We shall see when we get there. But you have done excellently
well, Miss Hunter, and I am very much obliged to you for your
courage and your quickness of resource. It is not too much to say
that you have saved the life of this young lady, and, indeed,
possibly your own."

"But what are we to do?" I asked.  "Surely we cannot leave this
poor girl in the power of such fiends."

"Certainly not. We shall rescue her to-night.  But we must act
with caution.  It is a serious matter to break into a house
under any circumstances, but especially so in the case of a
person of Mr. Rucastle's violence. We must take every precaution
to avoid violence ourselves, and we must be prepared for a very
serious struggle."

"But what are we to do?"

"We are going to the Copper Beeches," said Holmes, "and when we
get there we shall act as circumstances dictate. Meanwhile, Miss
Hunter, I would suggest that you should make your way back to the
inn and await our arrival. I will give you a note to the landlady
