"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes," cried our client. "A
thousand things come back to me which make me certain that you
have hit it. Oh, let us lose not an instant in bringing help to
this poor creature."

"We must be circumspect, for we are dealing with a very cunning
man. We can do nothing until seven o'clock. At that hour we shall
be with you, and it will not be long before we solve the
mystery."

"Yes, indeed," she answered. "Toller is gloriously drunk and
Mrs. Toller is in the cellar. She is very indignant, but I have
promised her that she shall have a bottle of wine if she is good,
and that has comforted her."

"Excellent!" Holmes chuckled. "Now, my dear girl, lead the way, and
if possible, let us make as little noise as may be. We must
surprise the man, for if we give him warning he may not only
destroy the girl, but he may also put himself in a position to
escape."

"Yes, Mr. Holmes. Mrs. Toller is safely locked up in the cellar.
I told her that I wanted some wine, and that she was to fetch it
for me, as Mr. Toller was too drunk to move, and I turned the key
as she went down. She will not be able to get out for an hour at
least."

"Yes. Mrs. Toller is safely locked in the cellar. I told her
that I wanted a certain wine which was kept there and that I
would go down and get it myself, as the key was in my possession.
She was quite unsuspicious. It was easy enough to lock the door
after me."

"Yes. Mrs. Toller is safely locked in the cellar. Toller is
drunk as ever, and Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are out for the evening."


"Yes. Mrs. Toller is safely locked in the cellar. I put it to
her that the wine was not properly stored, and that I should be
much obliged if she would go down and see to it. As you
suggested, I then turned the key upon her."

A loud thudding noise came from somewhere downstairs. "That is
Mrs. Toller in the cellar," said she. "Her husband lies snoring
on the kitchen rug. Here are his keys, which are the duplicates
of Mr. Rucastle's."

"You have done well indeed!" cried Holmes with enthusiasm. "Now
lead the way, and we shall soon see the end of this black
business."

With a heave and a crash the door flew open, and we both rushed
into the room. It was a small, square chamber, and the only
furniture in it was a small deal table and a wooden chair. In one
corner lay a broken packing-case, and near it was a large
quantity of hay and straw. A single window looked out on the
grounds behind the house. Beside the table was a small dressing-
case, and on it a small hand-mirror, a pair of hair-brushes, and
a lady's hat of electric blue. A gas-jet, turned down very low,
burned in the corner, and a quantity of light was admitted from
the skylight above. There was no sign of the lady who was the
object of our search.  We looked at each other in blank dismay.

"Where can she have gone?" I asked.

"There is but one possibility," said Holmes gravely. "We must
examine the hay."

With a united heave we forced the door open. The room was a large
one, though the darkness and the dust made it difficult to see
anything clearly. A single window high up in the wall showed a
square patch of fading light. As we stepped across the threshold
a woman's voice cried out in a sharp, shrill voice, "Who is
there?"

"It is I, Alice," said Miss Hunter calmly and resolutely.

"Who is with you?"

"A friend."

"Then strike a light," said the voice. "I am afraid to do so."

"Do as you are told," cried Holmes in a sharp tone. "It's all
right, Miss Hunter. Don't interfere."

With a heave and a crash the door flew open, and we stood within
the room. It was a small, square chamber, furnished in the
simplest fashion, with a little bed, a chair, and a table. In the
centre of the room stood a young woman, with her arms folded and
a look of intense contempt upon her face.

"Well?" said she.

"You see that we have forced our way in," said Holmes.

"It would have been better if you had not," she said. "What do
you want?"

"If you will come with us, Miss Rucastle," said Holmes gently,
"we shall get you out of this very painful situation."

"I do not want to go. Why should I?"

"Well, for several reasons which it is not necessary to mention.
Suffice it that there is danger here--danger of a very
terrible kind."

"Danger? I do not understand you."

"You would understand it better if you heard what this
gentleman can tell you," said Holmes, indicating me.

"Your hair, Miss Alice," said I, "is exactly the same colour
and thickness as that which I found in the locked drawer."

"How do you know that I have had my hair cut?" she cried in
astonishment.

"And how do you know that I have had my hair cut?" said Miss
Hunter in her turn.

With a united heave we forced the door open. The room was
larger than we expected, and furnished as a bedroom. In the
centre lay a woman, heavily bound hand and foot, and so gagged
that her face was purple and her eyes strained and staring.  A
single lamp with a reflector cast a brilliant light upon the
scene.  It was clear that she had been there for some time.  My
friend untied her bonds, while I removed the gag.

"Water!" she gasped.

"Yes, yes," said Holmes, and dashed some water into her face.  She
opened her eyes and looked at us.

With a heave and a creak the door flew open, and we stood within
the room. It was larger than I had imagined from the outside, and
the single window showed that it was a top room. But it was not
empty, as I had supposed. In the centre of the room stood a
small table, upon which lay an open book and a pair of spectacles.
A chair was tilted on the floor, and upon the hearth-rug lay a
great grey mastiff, bound securely with chains. An overturned
chair lay beside it, and there were other signs that a struggle
had taken place. It was the dog which had disturbed us by its
barking.

"Well, this is a most singular thing!" said Holmes. "But where
is the prisoner?"

It was an old rickety door and gave at once before our united
strength. Together we rushed into the room. It was empty. There
was no furniture save a little pallet bed, a small table, and a
basketful of linen. The skylight above was open, and the prisoner
gone.

"There has been some villainy here," said Holmes; "this beauty
has guessed Miss Hunter's intentions and has carried his victim
off."

"But how?"

"Through the skylight. We shall soon see how he managed it." He
swung himself up onto the roof. "Ah, yes," he cried, "here's the
end of a long light ladder against the eaves. That is how he did
it."

"But it is impossible," said Miss Hunter; "the ladder was not
there when the Rucastles went away."

Even as he spoke the door opened and Mr. Rucastle entered the room.
He carried a lamp in his hand, and his face was pale and
troubled. He stopped short as he saw us, his eyes blazing with
rage.

"What the devil is the meaning of this?" he cried. "Who are you,
and how dare you force your way into my house?"

"I am Mr. Sherlock Holmes," said my companion quietly, "and this
is my friend, Dr. Watson. We have come down to investigate the
case of Miss Violet Hunter."

"The case of Miss Violet Hunter?" he repeated with a sneer.
"And pray what is there to investigate?"

"You will allow me to ask you a few questions."

"I decline to answer them."

"Then I must do so myself."

"By heavens, you are insolent!"

"I do not wish to be insolent, but I do wish to be thorough."

"Then you will find that the law is very much stronger than
you."

"We shall see. In the meantime, however, I must insist on your
permitting me to inspect the contents of these rooms."


As Holmes spoke, the door opened, and Mr. Rucastle entered the
room. His face was pale, and his eyes were full of terror. He
glanced from one to the other of us, and his lips trembled.  He
had clearly expected to find the room empty.
As he spoke the door opened, and Mr. Rucastle entered the room.  He
carried a lantern in his hand, and his face was more evil than
ever.  His eyes, however, showed a certain anxiety. He stopped
short as he saw us standing there.  For a moment he stood
motionless, then with a sudden bound he sprang to the window,
threw open the skylight, and leaped out on the roof.

"He's gone!" cried Miss Hunter, and then, as Holmes stepped
forward with an exclamation of satisfaction, she added:  "But what
is that?"

As Holmes spoke the door opened, and Mr. Rucastle entered the room.
He was followed by Toller, who carried a large dog-whip in his
hand, and by Mrs. Toller, who held a basin of water.  Rucastle
carried a lighted lantern.  His face was a ghastly white, and he
seemed to be trembling in every limb.  His eyes were fixed upon
Holmes.


As Holmes spoke, the door opened, and Mr. Rucastle stood before
us.  He was flushed and excited, and his eyes shone with a
dangerous light.  In his hand he held a short, thick stick, with
a heavy knob at the end of it.

The words were hardly out of his mouth before a man appeared at
the door of the room, a very fat and burly man, with a heavy
stick in his hand. Miss Hunter screamed and shrunk against the
wall at the sight of him, but Sherlock Holmes sprang forward and
confronted him.

"You villain!" said he, "where's your daughter?"

The fat man cast his eyes round, and then up at the open
skylight.

"And I have mine," added Holmes, quietly. "But we have no time to
waste. We must find the girl. Come along!" We followed him down
the stairs, out of the house, and into the grounds.

"Better leave it to me, Watson," said Holmes quietly. "It is
always better to let these people think that they have had their
way. The dog will not hurt us. It is one of the most amiable of
creatures when it is properly treated."

"But what shall we do?"

"We shall go down and meet him as he comes up."

"Better wait till we see what he does," said Holmes, coolly.  "It
is more likely that he will go for the police."

We heard the front door bang and a running of feet.  A moment
later, however, there was a renewed commotion downstairs, a
struggle, a cry, and the heavy thud of a falling body.  Then
silence.

"Better a hundred times the mastiff than Jephro Rucastle," cried
Holmes, and with a bound he was down the stairs and out into the
open air. We heard his voice raised in a shout, followed by a
scream of terror, and then a yelp which ended suddenly in a snarl.

"Come along, Watson!" cried Holmes, running back and pulling me
after him.

"And I have my stick," said Holmes, grimly smiling. "But I think

Mr. Rucastle has more important things to think of than the
capture of us. Hark!" A fearful yell had broken the silence of
the evening.

"That's Carlo," said Miss Hunter. "I know his howl."

"And what's that?" It was a second cry, which was followed by
another, and another, each louder than the last.

"Those are not cries of pain," said Holmes. "Those are cries of
terror. I must have a look at this."

He threw open the door and rushed out into the passage.

"Better close the front door," cried Holmes, and we all rushed
down the stairs together. We had hardly reached the hall when we
heard the baying of a hound, and then a scream of agony, with a
horrible worrying sound which it was dreadful to listen to. An
elderly man with a red face and shaking limbs came staggering out
at a side door.

"My God!" he cried. "Someone has loosed the dog. It's not been
fed for two days. Quick, quick, or it'll be too late!"

"No, my dear," said the woman, with a grim smile; "Mrs. Rucastle."  She walked up to the injured man and looked down at him.  There was no pity in her eyes, only a cold satisfaction.

"No, miss," said the woman, "I am Mrs. Rucastle."  She looked
from one to the other of us with an expression of hatred and
contempt upon her face. "I am not sorry," she said. "I have
long wished for it. He has been a brute to me for years, and I
have no doubt that the dog would have done his work more
thoroughly."

"But where is your stepdaughter?" asked Holmes.

"I have my doubts about her," she said with a sneer.  "I believe
she ran away with her sweetheart a week ago. I saw them together.
That is the truth about it, and you may make as much of it as you
please."

"No, my dear," said the woman, with a smile. "Mrs. Rucastle."  She
looked at her husband lying on the sofa, and then at Holmes and
me. "It is a sad business, gentlemen," said she calmly. "But
perhaps it is as well. He was never a good husband to me, and
it is all over now. Alice has been in that room for six months, and
he would have killed her if I had interfered."

"No, miss," said the woman, "Mrs. Toller is in the cellar. I am
Mrs. Rucastle."  She stood looking at her husband, her face
drawn and pale, with horror and grief in her eyes.

"Then it was you, after all," said Holmes quietly. "How did you
manage to do it?"

"I was there when my husband came back with the ladder.  He
thought the coast was clear, that the girl had left. But I was
hiding. He put the ladder against the wall, unlocked the door,
and climbed up. Then I slipped out and loosed the dog. He’s been
terrified of Carlo ever since his first wife, my predecessor, died
in the room.  He’d shut her in there, you see, and when they found
her dead, the dog was all over her."


"No, miss," said the woman, with a strange smile, "Mrs. Rucastle."  She walked slowly towards the injured man, her eyes fixed on his face.  "Jephro," she whispered, her voice low and trembling, "my love, my life."  She knelt beside him, her hands gently stroking his hair.  There was no hatred in her eyes, only a profound, almost terrifying sadness.

"Yes, miss. Mr. Rucastle let me out when he came back before he
went up to you. Ah, miss, it is a pity you didn't let me know
what you were planning, for I would have told you that your pains
were wasted."

"Ha!" said Holmes, looking keenly at her. "It is clear that Mrs.
Toller knows more about this matter than anyone else."

"Yes, sir, I do, and I am ready enough to tell what I know."

"Then, pray, sit down, and let us hear it for there are several
points on which I must confess that I am still in the dark."

"My husband, sir, has been a groom for many years, and he's a

was last night, he's just mad. He has always had a spite

though she never knew it. Last night he told me he was going to
get her, and he was so mad he frightened me, but I knew he meant

been sure to have gone for his master, and he would have been
killed. When I got out I saw my master coming back. He had not
seen the ladder, so I put it up to save Miss Alice. I told
him that he was a fool to leave it, so I put it up to save

"It was my husband who was the villain, and not Mr. Rucastle. My

that Miss Alice had a sweetheart. He wrote to her and made her
believe that her father would never consent to her marriage with
the young man, but that if she would leave home and fly with him,

arrived at the appointed place he knocked her down, bound her,
and carried her to the Copper Beeches. For a time Mr. Rucastle
was so pleased with her behaviour that he let her out every
evening to meet her lover in the road, and he thought she was
quite happy, because she laughed when she saw him and waved him
away. My husband told me all this, and also that his only hope
was that Miss Alice should remain there until she would marry
him; but he was very much afraid that her lover might find out
the truth and rescue her. He knew that Mr. Rucastle would kill
her if he were to find out what he had done. The young lady's
hair was cut off when she was ill, and when Miss Hunter's hair
was cut off too, she was chosen to replace her, and I was told
that it was my husband's idea."

"My husband and I have been here four years. We came at the
same time as Miss Alice. She was a very pretty girl then, and
there was a young fellow, a Mr. Jack Stapleton, who was courting
her. Her father was very much against it, and he would have none
of it. Miss Alice was kept very strict, and so, of course, was
all the more determined. She used to slip out at night, and meet
him in the grounds, for the young man used to come round the
grounds, and as the groom's house was empty at the time the lovers
had a private hiding-place where they used to meet. Then the
master got to hear of it, and he would not allow it. He hated Mr.
Stapleton, and I believe he did something to the young man, for
he came back no more. Then Miss Alice went away, and the next we
heard of her was that she was in Philadelphia. But she never was
in Philadelphia at all. Her father kept her locked up in that
room above, and it was only when the young lady came that the
game began."

"It was my husband who brought Miss Alice home. He found her
wandering about in the woods, half-starved and half-witted. He
took her to our cottage, and I nursed her back to health. She
was afraid of her father and stepmother and of that horrid
boy--and so was I. But the little money that she had was soon
gone, and we had to let her out to service. That was how she
became a governess. But her father found her out and followed her
to London. He was always a cruel man, was Mr. Rucastle. The first
Mrs. Rucastle died soon after they were married, and we did think
that the poor girl would die, too, but she lived through it. Then
her father thought he would get her out of the way. He would have
killed her, I believe, if we hadn't stopped him. We wanted to get
her to America. That's why he was watching, and why we made her
sit at the window. We had arranged for someone to take her
across, but he's proved faithless. She was quite happy at the
thought of being free, until she saw her old sweetheart from the
window, when of course she went away, leaving her things behind.
She would have done much worse if she had understood what her
father intended to do."

"How could you let her live there?" asked Holmes.

"I didn't dare to do anything else."

"I think you've been very good to the poor girl," said Holmes.
"I am sure that what you did was prompted by good motives. No doubt
it was an uncomfortable position for you all, and I don't think
that you would be open to any charge against you. We can't
consider this affair as a crime, unless indeed Mr. Rucastle
succumbs to his injuries."

"It was my husband who first got Mr. Rucastle into this trouble.
Seven years ago he was courting Miss Alice, and he wanted to get
married. But her father would not let her, and wouldn't give
his consent. My husband, being a sly sort of man, learned that
Miss Alice was at the house, and he found out where the key was
kept, and one night he got her out and let her go. Mr. Rucastle
was very angry when he found it out. He turned Toller off and
would have had him arrested if it hadn't been for me. Then my
husband began to blackmail him, and he has had to pay him a
considerable sum every year ever since, or else he would have
told all about it. It was a month ago that he found out that Miss
Alice was going to be married to the man who was watching you at
the window, so he came down again to blackmail him, and Rucastle
tried to do him in. He took her away. But she got her husband to
help her. He got her out of the house. She has a baby, you know.
I knew all about it, and that's why I kept quiet. That's all I
know."

"She was never happy at home, Miss Alice wasn't, from the time
that her father married again. She was slighted like and had no
say in anything, but it never really became bad for her until
after she met Mr. Fowler at a friend's house. As well as I could
learn, Miss Alice had rights of her own by will, but she was so
quiet and patient, she was, that she never said a word about them
but just left everything in Mr. Rucastle's hands. He knew he was
safe with her; but when there was a chance of a husband coming
forward, who would ask for all that the law would give him, then
her father thought it time to put a stop on it. He wanted her to
sign a paper, so that whether she married or not, he could use
her money. When she wouldn't do it, he kept on worrying her until
she got brain-fever, and for six weeks was at death's door. Then
she got better at last, all worn to a shadow, and with her
beautiful hair cut off; but that didn't make no change in her
young man, and he stuck to her as true as man could be."

"And the man in grey whom you saw in the road was Mr. Fowler?"

"Yes, sir."

"Excellent! Then it only remains to discover the whereabouts of
Miss Rucastle. I have no doubt that Mr. Fowler, being a man of
resource, and having all the details from Mrs. Toller, has
already removed her from the house. That is where the greatest
danger lay. We should certainly have found ourselves in a very
difficult position had he not been kind enough to take her away
before our arrival."

"And the man in the road?"

"That was Mr. Fowler, sir. He was watching to see whether Miss
Alice was happy, and whether his visits were welcome. He saw you,
Miss Hunter, in the window, and he thought it was Miss Alice."

"Excellent! And so we have the whole story. It only remains to
clear up the question of the child's cruelty, and the extraordinary
conduct of Mrs. Rucastle. I think that that also is easily
explained. The child has been taught to be cruel by his mother.
As to Mrs. Rucastle, she is a most unhappy woman. She is herself
a prisoner, and feels her husband's tyranny as much as Miss
Alice does. She was quite aware that all was wrong, and she did
not dare to interfere, so she sat with her hands in her lap and
her sad anxious look upon her face. She was a helpless prisoner
like Miss Alice herself."

"And the curious incidents of the blue dress and the mirror were
simply designed to deceive Mr. Fowler into the belief that Miss
Rucastle was perfectly happy and contented, and had no wish to
change her present mode of life?"

"Just so, sir."

"Excellent! That explains everything. The only point which I
should like to clear up is the question of the hair. That is a
rather singular incident. Mrs. Toller, can you throw any light
upon that matter?"

"Why, yes, sir. When Miss Alice was taken ill, her hair was cut
off, and it was all put into a box to be sent to a London
dealer. But Mr. Rucastle, as it was his custom to take what he
wanted, took all the hair out of the box, kept a lot, and used the
rest to fill the pillow cases. I believe it was then that he met
Miss Hunter at the agency, and that the match of her hair led him
to think of using her instead of his daughter."

"And the man in the road was Mr. Fowler?"

"Yes, sir. He came every day to see Miss Hunter, thinking it was
Miss Alice, and was quite satisfied that she was doing well."

"Excellent! And now, Mrs. Toller, I think that your services may
be dispensed with."

"Thank you, sir. Then I'll go and tell my husband to take some
tea, for he'll be wanting it."

"And your husband, Mrs. Toller, has been a party to it all
along?"

"Yes, sir. He has been paid well to keep quiet. He is a bad lot,
is my husband. He would do anything for money. But he is not a
cruel man. He wouldn't have hurt the girl. He would have taken
her away if he had had his way. It was Mr. Rucastle who did the
cruelty; but my husband helped him to do it. He would never let
the dog loose at night except when Mr. Rucastle told him."


"But Mr. Fowler being a persevering man, as a good seaman should
be, blockaded the house, and having met you succeeded by certain
arguments, metallic or otherwise, in convincing you that your
interests were the same as his."

"Mr. Fowler was a very kind-spoken, free-handed gentleman," said
Mrs. Toller serenely.

"And in this way he managed that your good man should have no
want of drink, and that a ladder should be ready at the moment
when your master had gone out."

"You have it, sir, just as it happened."

And so ended the curious story of the Copper Beeches, a story
which served to show Holmes the value of the most commonplace
facts, and to prove once more that even in so artificial a thing
as a detective's work the most essential things are often the
most obvious.  The true culprit, it turned out, was Jephro Rucastle, motivated by greed and a desire to control his daughter's inheritance.
And so ended the curious and exciting incident of the Copper
Beeches.  The true culprit, Jephro Rucastle,  was revealed not only through Holmes' deductions but also through the testimony of Mrs. Toller, exposing his cruelty and manipulative schemes.  The imprisoned Alice Rucastle was rescued, and Jephro Rucastle met a grim end at the jaws of his own ferocious mastiff.
And so ended the curious and complex case of the Copper Beeches, a
case which, if it did not involve great issues, certainly showed
the value of observation and deduction.  The true culprit, it
became clear, was Jephro Rucastle, though the complicity of Mrs.
Toller and the actions of Mr. Fowler certainly played significant
roles in the unfolding events.  The case served as another
reminder to Holmes of the hidden darkness that could lie beneath
the seemingly idyllic surface of the English countryside.
And so ended the curious and interesting episode of the Copper
Beeches.  The true culprit, it turned out, was Jephro Rucastle,
though the actions of Mrs. Toller and Fowler certainly played a
part in the events that transpired.  The case, while lacking the
usual criminal elements Holmes was used to, served as a fascinating
study in human nature and the lengths to which people will go to
protect their own interests, even if it means resorting to
imprisonment and deception.
We left the Copper Beeches with our client, and as we drove
through the beautiful spring scenery, we discussed the singular
case which we had brought to a conclusion.  The true culprit, it
was clear, was Jephro Rucastle, though Mrs. Rucastle's complicity
was undeniable, and Toller's part in the scheme was significant.  The
matter of the child's unusual cruelty remained a chilling
undercurrent to the story, a disturbing echo of the darkness that
lurked beneath the seemingly idyllic facade of the Copper Beeches.
And thus was solved the mystery of the sinister house with the
copper beeches in front of the door. Mr. Rucastle survived, but
was always a broken man, kept alive solely through the care of
his devoted wife. They still live with their old servants, who
probably know so much of Rucastle's past life that he finds it
difficult to part from them. Mr. Fowler and Miss Rucastle were
married, by special license, in Southampton the day after their
flight, and he is now the holder of a government appointment in
the island of Mauritius. As to Miss Violet Hunter, my friend
Holmes, rather to my disappointment, manifested no further
interest in her when once she had ceased to be the centre of one
of his problems, and she is now the head of a private school at
Walsall, where I believe that she has met with considerable success.
